meta.blurb: On 7 January 1610, Galileo saw three small stars in a line beside Jupiter. Four days later he knew they were circling it. His short book tells the story and adds mountains on the Moon and a sky full of new stars.
meta.bible: Galileo Galilei: Italian mathematician and professor at Padua, born 1564 in Pisa, died 1642; author of Sidereus Nuncius, the Sidereal Messenger or Starry Messenger, a short Latin book printed in Venice in March 1610. Padua: the university town where he taught. Venice: the city where the book was printed and the spyglass was shown to its leaders in August 1609. Florence: the city of the Medici, where he moved in 1610. Cosimo II de' Medici: the young Grand Duke of Tuscany, once Galileo's pupil, to whom the book is dedicated. Medicean Stars: Galileo's name for the four moons of Jupiter, in honour of the Medici family. Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto: the names used today, suggested by Simon Marius. Johannes Kepler: the German astronomer who replied warmly in 1610. Aristotle: the Greek thinker whose picture of a perfect, unchanging heaven most scholars followed. Copernicus: the Polish astronomer who proposed the Sun at the centre in 1543. Jesuit astronomers of Rome confirmed the discoveries. Dutch: the spyglass was first made in the Netherlands. Key terms: Spyglass, Telescope, Lens, Lenses, Crater, Craters, Crescent, Constellation, Nebulae, Orbit, Praesepe, Pleiades, Orion, Milky Way, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Moon, Earth, Sun, Earthshine. Facts: first lenses made things look about three times closer, later ones about twenty and nearly thirty times; about five hundred and fifty copies were printed; the Moon's mountains were reckoned at over four miles, which was too high; the Pleiades drawing shows thirty-six stars. Voice and tone: eager, clear and exact, a report of what one person saw, night by night, with the dates and the evidence; where Galileo guessed, the text says so.

B1B2: In March 1610, a professor named Galileo Galilei published a short book in Venice called The Sidereal Messenger. In it he reported things in the sky that no human being had ever seen before.

In Galileo's day, most scholars followed the Greek thinker Aristotle, who taught that the heavens were perfect and never changed. They also believed that the Earth stood still at the centre of everything, with the Sun, Moon and stars moving around it.

More than sixty years earlier, a Polish astronomer named Copernicus had suggested that the Sun, and not the Earth, is at the centre. Most people thought the idea absurd, and nobody could prove it either way.

In 1609, news reached Galileo in Venice that a man in the Netherlands had made a tube with glass lenses. Looking through it, far-off things seemed to be near, and Galileo decided to build one himself.
Galileo worked out how glass bends light and fitted two lenses into a tube made of lead. His first spyglass made things look three times closer, which was not yet enough to astonish anyone.

Galileo ground and polished lenses himself, choosing only the best pieces of glass. After many tries, he built a spyglass that made things look about twenty times closer, and later one that reached nearly thirty times.
In August 1609, Galileo took his spyglass to the top of a bell tower in Venice and showed it to the city's leaders. They could see ships far out at sea hours before the naked eye could make them out.
The Senate was so pleased that it gave Galileo his teaching post at Padua for life, with a much higher salary. The leaders saw the spyglass as a tool for trade and war, but Galileo had other plans.
Then Galileo did something that few people had thought of: he pointed the spyglass at the sky. Late in 1609, on clear nights in Padua, he turned it first to the Moon.

Followers of Aristotle said that the Moon was a perfectly smooth ball. Through the glass, Galileo saw that it was rough, with dark patches, bright patches and shapes that looked like mountains and hollows.

At half Moon, Galileo noticed that the line between the lit part and the dark part was not smooth. It was ragged and wavy, just as the edge of the light would be across a mountainous country on Earth.

Galileo saw small bright points shining in the dark part of the Moon, some distance from the lit edge. As the light spread, they grew and joined the lit area, like mountain tops catching the first rays of the morning.
Across the Moon, Galileo found wide round hollows with raised rims, and the Sun's light threw dark shadows inside them. He compared one huge hollow to Bohemia, a whole country ringed by mountains.

By measuring the length of a mountain's shadow and using geometry, Galileo calculated how tall the lunar mountains must be. He reckoned that some rose higher than four miles, although his figure was a little too large.

Galileo decided that the Moon is not a perfect, smooth ball but a world with hills, valleys and plains, rather like Earth. This was a shock to people who thought the heavens were quite unlike the ground beneath their feet.

When the Moon is a thin crescent, its dark part can still be seen glowing faintly. Galileo explained that this glow is sunlight bouncing off the Earth, which lights the Moon just as the Moon lights us.

This meant that the Earth is also a bright body in the sky, much like the Moon and the planets. For Galileo it was a strong hint that the Earth is not a special place at the centre, but one of the wanderers.

Galileo then turned his glass on the stars, and he noticed something strange about them. The planets grew into small round discs, but the stars stayed as tiny points of light, which meant that they must be unimaginably far away.
The telescope showed more stars than anyone had imagined. Galileo wrote that for every star known before, he could now see more than ten new ones that the naked eye had never found.

He tried to draw the whole constellation of Orion but found that there were far too many new stars. So he drew only the Belt and the Sword, and marked dozens of faint stars that no one had ever noticed.
Most people can see only six or seven stars in the little group called the Pleiades. Galileo's glass revealed dozens more, and he drew thirty-six of them in his book.
Astronomers had long noticed pale, cloudy patches in the sky, which they called nebulae. Galileo looked at one called the Praesepe and saw that it was a cluster of many small stars.

For ages people had argued about what the Milky Way is: a cloud, a mist or something else. Galileo looked and saw that it is made of a huge number of stars, too faint and close together to see one by one.
Galileo drew the Moon in soft brown ink, painting the light and the shadows so that readers could see what he had seen. He wanted everyone to be able to check his claims for themselves.

On the evening of 7 January 1610, Galileo looked at the bright planet Jupiter and noticed three tiny stars close beside it. Two stood on one side of the planet and one on the other, and Galileo thought little of them at first.

The next night, Galileo looked again and was surprised: all three small stars were now on the western side of Jupiter. He supposed that the planet must have moved, but the books said that it should be moving the other way.
On 10 January, only two of the stars were visible, and both lay to the east of Jupiter. Galileo wondered whether the third was hidden behind the planet, and a doubt began to grow in his mind.

By 11 January, Galileo was sure that the little stars were not fixed in the sky. They were travelling around Jupiter, changing places from night to night, and he realised that he had found something completely new.
On 13 January, Galileo saw a fourth tiny star near the planet for the first time. Now there were four, and all of them stayed close to Jupiter wherever it travelled across the sky.
Galileo watched Jupiter on every clear night and drew where the four stars stood. Clouds and cold sometimes spoiled his work, but the drawings slowly built up a clear pattern.
Galileo gave reasons why they could not be ordinary stars. They always stayed close to Jupiter and in almost a straight line, and they changed places in a regular way.
He saw that the moon nearest to Jupiter swept back and forth fastest, while the farthest one moved much more slowly. This was just how small worlds circling a larger one should behave.
Sometimes a moon vanished from view, hidden behind Jupiter or lost in its glare, and then it came back again. These comings and goings fitted a round-and-round motion perfectly.
Here was a planet moving through the sky with four moons of its own. It showed that not everything in the heavens circles the Earth, which was a serious blow to the old view.

Some critics said that the Earth could not be moving round the Sun, because it would lose its Moon on the way. Jupiter, Galileo replied, carries four moons with it on its long journey around the Sun and loses none.

Galileo named the four new bodies the Medicean Stars, in honour of Cosimo II de' Medici, the young ruler of Tuscany, and his three brothers. He hoped that the Medici family would reward him for the gift.
The book begins with a warm dedication to Cosimo II, who had once been Galileo's pupil. Galileo compared the Medici family to the bright new stars that now shone beside Jupiter.

Galileo wrote the book in a great hurry, because he wanted to be first to announce his discoveries. About five hundred and fifty copies were printed in Venice in March 1610, and they sold out almost at once.
Letters and copies of the book travelled quickly across Europe. The astronomer Johannes Kepler wrote a warm reply, saying that he believed Galileo even though he had not seen the moons himself.
Not everyone was pleased, because some scholars said that the lenses were tricking the eye. According to Galileo, a few of them even refused to look through the glass at all.
To be fair, the new instrument was hard to use. The view was narrow and shaky, and Galileo himself advised that the tube should be fixed firmly so that the hand could not shake it.
Before long, other skilled observers made telescopes and began to look for themselves. The Jesuit astronomers in Rome confirmed the discoveries, and in 1611 they welcomed Galileo with honour.
Cosimo II rewarded Galileo with a new post in the summer of 1610. Galileo left Padua for Florence as the Grand Duke's Mathematician and Philosopher, which gave him money and time for his work.

Later in 1610, Galileo found that Saturn seemed to have two odd lumps beside it, and that Venus goes through phases like the Moon. These discoveries came after the little book, but they came from the same instrument.
The Moon had mountains, Jupiter had moons, and the Milky Way was a sea of stars. Taken together, these discoveries made the old view of a perfect and simple heaven very hard to believe.
Galileo did not ask his readers to take his word for it. He described what he had done, drew what he had seen, and invited anyone with a good spyglass to look and judge for themselves.
Galileo's support for Copernicus later brought him into conflict with the Church. In 1633 he was tried in Rome for defending a moving Earth, and he lived under house arrest until he died.
The names Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto were suggested by Simon Marius, who also said that he had seen the moons in 1610. Dozens of smaller moons of Jupiter have been found since.

In 1995 a spacecraft named Galileo arrived at Jupiter and spent almost eight years studying the planet and its moons. Long before, between 1969 and 1972, astronauts had walked on the Moon and found the mountains and craters that Galileo first saw.
The Sidereal Messenger is a very short book, yet it changed astronomy for ever. It shows what can happen when someone makes a better tool, looks carefully, and tells the truth about what he sees.
C1C2: In March 1610, a mathematics professor from Padua named Galileo Galilei published in Venice a slim Latin book with an extraordinary title, Sidereus Nuncius, which means the Sidereal Messenger or the Starry Messenger. It announced discoveries made with a new instrument, and it did so in a plain and eager voice, as though the author could hardly wait to share what he had seen. Within a few weeks the whole educated world of Europe was talking about it, and the first printing had almost sold out.

In the Europe of Galileo's youth, the educated majority still followed the teaching of Aristotle, who had declared that the heavens were made of a perfect, unchanging substance quite unlike the ordinary stuff of the Earth. The Earth, it was held, stood motionless at the centre of the universe, while the Sun, the Moon, the planets and the stars wheeled around it in flawless circles. It was a beautiful scheme, and it had survived for nearly two thousand years.

More than sixty years before Galileo's book, the Polish astronomer Copernicus had proposed an alarming alternative, namely that the Sun stands at the centre and the Earth is only one of several planets circling it. Mathematicians admired the neatness of his calculations, but the great majority of scholars dismissed the idea as contrary to common sense and to scripture. Until the autumn of 1609, however, nobody could point to a single observation that settled the matter one way or the other.

In the summer of 1609, while visiting Venice, Galileo heard a rumour that a Dutchman had made an instrument which brought distant objects close to the eye. Some people dismissed it as a mere toy, but Galileo was a man who could see a use for any new device, and he was curious to know how it worked. He hurried back to Padua, determined to build one of his own and to discover for himself whether the tale could be true.

Galileo did not simply copy the rumour; he thought about the way glass bends light, and within days he had fitted two lenses into a tube of lead, one curved outward and the other curved inward. The first instrument made things appear about three times nearer than they really were, which was hardly enough to excite anyone. It persuaded him, however, that much more could be done, and he went back to his workbench.

The great difficulty lay in the glass itself, and so Galileo taught himself to grind and polish lenses with great patience, throwing away every piece that was flawed. Step by step his instruments grew stronger, until one of them made distant things look about twenty times closer and a later one nearly thirty times. Few makers anywhere could match them, and Galileo soon became known across Italy as a master of the craft.

In August 1609, Galileo carried his spyglass to the top of a tall bell tower in Venice and invited the leaders of the republic to look out over the lagoon. Through the little tube they could pick out ships that were still far beyond the horizon, and the senators were quick to see how valuable such a device might prove at sea and in war. The demonstration was a triumph in every way, though even as the senators applauded Galileo was already thinking of much larger things.

The Senate rewarded him generously, confirming him in his professorship at Padua for life and raising his salary considerably. The senators saw in the spyglass a weapon for the defence of the republic and a help to its merchants, but Galileo had begun to wonder what it might reveal if it were pointed upward. That question was to occupy him through the autumn and the winter, and the answer would be far more valuable to the world than any gift from the Senate.

Late in 1609, on a clear night in Padua, Galileo did what no one had yet thought to do with the new device, and turned it upon the heavens. He began with the Moon, which hung bright and close above the rooftops, and he looked for a long time before he dared to trust what he saw. For several weeks afterwards he returned to it whenever the sky was clear, making notes and drawings by the light of a lamp.

The followers of Aristotle had taught that the Moon was a perfect, polished sphere, without blemish or roughness of any kind. Through the glass, Galileo saw instead a scarred and uneven surface, with broad dark patches, brighter regions and a crowd of shapes that looked remarkably like mountains and valleys. The Moon, he reported with evident excitement, was far more like the Earth than any scholar of his day had ever supposed.

Observing the Moon at its first quarter, Galileo noticed that the boundary between the bright and dark parts was not a clean, even curve, as it would be on a smooth ball. It was ragged and indented, with bright tongues running into the shadow and dark patches lying within the light. This was precisely how a rough landscape ought to look as the Sun rose across it.

In the darkness beyond the line of light, Galileo saw small points of brightness, which grew as the hours passed and at last joined the lit surface. They were the summits of lunar mountains, he concluded, catching the rays of the rising Sun while the valleys at their feet were still in shadow. Anyone who has watched dawn touch the peaks of the Alps will recognise the scene.

All over the Moon Galileo found wide, round hollows with raised rims, which we now call craters, and as the Sun climbed higher the shadows inside them shrank and slid across their floors. One enormous hollow made him think of Bohemia, a whole country enclosed by a ring of mountains. His readers, most of whom had never seen a mountain from a distance, could hardly have pictured a stranger place.

Galileo was not content merely to describe what he saw, and so he measured the length of the shadows cast by lunar mountains and used simple geometry to work out their heights. He reckoned that some of them rose to more than four miles, which would make them higher than any mountain on Earth. Later astronomers found that he had overestimated their height, but his method was sound, and it is still used in a refined form today.

Galileo drew from his observations a daring conclusion, namely that the Moon is no polished heavenly lantern but a rugged world with hills, valleys and plains, not unlike our own. The division that scholars had drawn between the perfect heavens and the imperfect Earth began to look arbitrary. If the Moon was made of rock and earth, then the sky might not be so different from the ground.

Every observer had noticed that when the Moon is a thin crescent, the rest of its disc can be seen glowing faintly, but no one had explained it satisfactorily. Galileo argued that this ghostly light, often called earthshine, is sunlight that has been reflected from the Earth onto the Moon, and he supported his idea with careful reasoning about the positions of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon. It was a lovely demonstration, he thought, that the two bodies shine upon each other like partners in a quiet exchange of light.

If the Earth could light the Moon, he reasoned, then seen from the Moon it would shine in the sky just as the Moon shines in ours. This was a quiet but important step, for it placed our world among the planets, as one shining body among others, and not in a privileged position apart. Galileo was careful not to say more than the evidence allowed, yet the hint was plain.

When Galileo turned his spyglass from the planets to the fixed stars, he noticed a curious difference between them. The planets swelled into small, round, sharply edged discs, much like miniature moons, but the stars remained tiny sparks of light, hardly enlarged at all. The stars, he concluded, must lie at distances so vast that even a magnifying power of thirty could not make them grow.

Wherever Galileo directed his tube, he found stars that no one had ever seen, for they are too faint for the naked eye to detect. He wrote that their numbers exceeded the known stars more than tenfold, and that the sky was far richer than anyone had suspected. It was a new universe, hidden until then simply because no instrument had been strong enough to reveal it.

Galileo had intended to draw the entire constellation of Orion, but the new stars were so numerous that he soon gave up the idea. He settled instead on the Belt and the Sword, a small patch of the sky, and in it he marked dozens of faint stars that had been invisible to every earlier observer. The drawing, printed in his book, remains a vivid piece of evidence of how much the heavens had been hiding from every earlier generation.

Most people can make out only six or seven stars in the small, glittering group known as the Pleiades, and the ancient poets had long loved it for that reason. Galileo's glass revealed a great many more, and he drew thirty-six of them in his book, with their positions marked as exactly as he could manage. The little cluster that had delighted poets for centuries turned out, under his lens, to be a true crowd of stars.

Astronomers had long known of certain pale, cloudy patches in the sky, which they called nebulae and supposed to be made of some thin, shining matter. When Galileo turned his glass on one of them, the Praesepe, the cloud dissolved into a close crowd of tiny stars, and he guessed that others would prove to be the same. Later astronomers found that he was right about some of them and wrong about others, which are real clouds of glowing gas.

For ages, philosophers had argued about the nature of the Milky Way, which some took to be a vapour, others a stream of milk and others a mere pale glow. Galileo pointed his spyglass at the broad band and found that it was composed of a vast number of stars, packed so closely together that the unaided eye could see only a glimmering mist. One of the oldest puzzles in astronomy had been settled in a single evening.

Galileo was a skilled draftsman, and he painted the Moon in soft washes of brown ink, catching the shadows of the craters and the glitter of the mountain tops with remarkable delicacy. The drawings were part of his argument, for they let a reader see what he had seen and judge the evidence without relying on his word. In an age of heavy authority, it was a quietly radical way of doing science.

On the evening of 7 January 1610, Galileo turned his spyglass on the brilliant planet Jupiter and noticed three small, bright stars lying close beside it. They stood in an almost perfectly straight line, two to the east of the planet and one to the west, and he took them for ordinary fixed stars. He could not have guessed that he was looking at the discovery of his life.

The following night, Galileo returned to his instrument and was startled to find that all three stars now lay to the west of Jupiter, and closer together than before. He supposed at first that the planet must have moved past them, but the astronomical tables said that Jupiter ought to be travelling in the opposite direction. Something, he began to suspect, was not quite as he had assumed, and the doubt was beginning to excite him.

On the tenth of January, after a cloudy interval, Galileo found only two stars, both of them now to the east of Jupiter, and the third had vanished. It occurred to him that it might be hidden behind the planet's disc, and with that thought the old explanation began to fall apart. Perhaps, he began to think, the stars were not fixed in the sky as he had supposed, and the puzzle deserved a closer look.

By the eleventh of January, Galileo had reached a conclusion that overturned his first assumption, which was that these bodies were not fixed stars at all but travellers moving around Jupiter. Night by night they changed their places on either side of the planet, exactly as small companions would if they were circling it. He had found something that no human being had known before, and he knew it.

On the thirteenth of January, Galileo saw for the first time a fourth tiny star close to Jupiter, which brought the number of its companions to four. All of them kept faithfully to the planet's side as it travelled across the sky from night to night. The pattern was far too regular, he saw, to be a mere accident of the sky, and he resolved to follow it every night.

For almost two months, Galileo watched Jupiter on every clear night and drew the positions of the four stars in a long series of small diagrams. Clouds and bitter cold interrupted him again and again, yet the pattern emerged unmistakably from the pages of his notebook. In the end he printed the diagrams in his book, so that readers could follow his reasoning night by night.

Galileo set out his reasons with care, for he knew that many readers would resist the conclusion. Ordinary stars, he pointed out, do not accompany a planet wherever it goes, nor do they keep to a straight line beside it or change places in such a regular manner. The only reasonable explanation, he concluded, was that these four bodies were circling Jupiter itself, held to the planet as the Moon is held to the Earth.

As his observations accumulated, Galileo noticed that the bodies closest to Jupiter swung to and fro most rapidly, while the most distant one took the longest to change its place. This was exactly how small worlds ought to behave when they circle a larger one, and he regarded it as strong support for his view. He did not yet know their exact periods, since that would require many more weeks of watching, but he understood the principle.

From time to time one of the bodies vanished altogether, having passed behind the planet or been lost in its glare, and after a while it returned, as a circling companion would. These comings and goings fitted a round-and-round motion perfectly, and they made every other explanation look strained. Galileo, watching them reappear on schedule night after night, felt that no reasonable doubt was left.

Here was a great planet moving across the sky, attended by four moons of its own, and so the old claim that every heavenly body circles the Earth could no longer be defended. Jupiter, it now seemed, was a centre of motion in its own right, and so the Earth was not the only one. The simple tidy universe of Aristotle suddenly seemed too small to hold the facts.

Critics of Copernicus had argued that if the Earth circled the Sun, it would leave the Moon far behind, and the very idea seemed absurd. Galileo pointed out that Jupiter, which was believed by many to travel around the Sun, carries four moons along with it on its long journey and loses none of them. The objection, he said, had lost its force, since the heavens plainly contained more than one centre of motion.

With a mixture of gratitude and ambition, Galileo named the four new bodies the Medicean Stars, in honour of Cosimo II de' Medici, the young Grand Duke of Tuscany, and his three brothers. It was a clever and generous gesture, and it was also an excellent way of attracting the interest of a powerful family. Galileo, who had been born near Pisa in Tuscany, had long hoped to return to Florence in a position of honour and independence.

The book opens with a warm and elaborate dedication to Cosimo II, whom Galileo had once taught in the summers, and it compares the glory of the Medici family with the brilliance of the new heavenly bodies. In the style of his time, he presented the discovery as a kind of gift to the prince. Modern readers may find the flattery excessive, but it was perfectly normal for the age.

Galileo wrote the book in a great hurry, working through January and February, because he wanted to be the first to announce his discoveries to the world. About five hundred and fifty copies came off the press in Venice in March 1610, and they sold so quickly that the supply was soon exhausted. In the space of a few weeks, a small and hurried book had become the sensation of the learned world.

Copies and letters travelled rapidly across Europe, carried by merchants, diplomats and scholars, and within weeks the discoveries were being debated from Prague to London. The German astronomer Johannes Kepler wrote a warm reply in which he declared that he believed Galileo's report, even though he had not yet seen the moons with his own eyes. Such open generosity from one of Europe's most respected astronomers pleased Galileo greatly, and it helped to persuade many others to take his claims seriously.

Not everyone welcomed the news, and some scholars insisted that the effects were mere tricks of the lenses, produced by the glass and not by anything in the sky. According to Galileo's own complaint, a few of them declined even to look through the spyglass, since they were sure that nothing new could be found in the heavens. The old view of the world was not going to be surrendered without a struggle.

To be fair to the doubters, the new instrument was difficult to use, for the field of view was narrow, the view trembled with every beat of the pulse, and it took practice to find the right object at all. Galileo himself advised that the tube should be fixed firmly so that the hand could not shake it. Many early failures to confirm his discoveries were probably a matter of poor technique.

Before long, other skilled observers built instruments of their own and began to look for themselves, and the doubters were gradually outnumbered. The Jesuit astronomers of the Roman College, who were among the best in Europe, confirmed the discoveries, and in 1611 they welcomed Galileo to Rome with real honour. By then the evidence of the moons of Jupiter could no longer be brushed aside.

In the summer of 1610, the Grand Duke Cosimo II rewarded Galileo with a handsome new position, and Galileo left Padua for Florence as Mathematician and Philosopher to the court. The post gave him a regular income and, most precious of all, the freedom to devote himself to research without the burden of lecturing. It was exactly the kind of position he had hoped to win, and it freed him to follow his discoveries wherever they might lead.

Later in 1610, Galileo discovered that Saturn appeared to have a pair of strange lumps on either side, and that Venus goes through phases like the Moon, from a thin crescent to a full disc. These discoveries came after the little book was printed, but they sprang from the same instrument and the same restless curiosity. Venus, in particular, was hard to reconcile with the old arrangement of the heavens.

The Moon had mountains, Jupiter had moons of its own and the Milky Way was a sea of stars, and each of these facts chipped away at the old view of the heavens. None of them proved that Copernicus was right, and Galileo, in this book, was cautious about saying so. Taken together, however, they made a perfect and unchanging heaven very hard to believe.

Galileo did not ask his readers simply to take his word for it, which in those days was an unusual approach to a scholarly question. He described what he had done, drew what he had seen and invited anyone with a good spyglass to look and judge for himself. Trust in the evidence, and not in famous names, was to become the foundation of modern science.

In later years Galileo's open support for the ideas of Copernicus brought him into serious conflict with the Church, which had come to regard the moving Earth as dangerous. In 1633, after the publication of a book that argued the case for it, he was tried in Rome and sentenced to spend the rest of his life under house arrest near Florence. He kept working to the end, and he wrote his last great book, on the science of motion, while confined to his home.

The names we now use for the four large moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, were proposed by a German astronomer, Simon Marius, who claimed that he had seen them independently in the same winter. Astronomers have since discovered dozens of smaller moons around Jupiter, so that Galileo's four proved to be only the largest of a great family. They are still called the Galilean moons in his honour, and they remain some of the most fascinating places in the solar system.

In 1995 a spacecraft named Galileo reached Jupiter, and for almost eight years it studied the planet, its storms and its moons at close range, sending back a vast amount of data. A quarter of a century earlier, astronauts had walked on the Moon itself and explored the mountains and craters that Galileo had first glimpsed through his little tube. In this way his observations had been confirmed, four centuries later, in the most direct way that anyone could imagine.

The Sidereal Messenger is only a few dozen pages long, yet it changed astronomy for ever and made the telescope the chief instrument of the science. It shows what can happen when a curious person builds a better tool, looks carefully and reports honestly what he finds, even when it contradicts the wisdom of the ages. Four hundred years later, we are still looking up, and still following the path that Galileo opened.
